L16: # EGFR/HER2 Vaccine Study
L17: 
L18: A new cancer immunotherapy developed by research team at Yale University is being evaluated in this study led by 【3†Therajan LLC †therajan.com】
L19: 
L20: 【4†Image†static.wixstatic.com】
L21: # Why immunotherapy?
L22: 
L23:   * May prevent the recurrence and spreading of cancer
L24: 
L25:   * May help when surgery is not possible, or if chemotherapy stops working
L26: 
L27:   * May slow or reverse cancer metastasis
L28: 
L29: 【5†Get Your Free Immunotherapy Guide†ccralliance.myflodesk.com】

L47:

L51: 
L52:   * "How these dogs recovered from lung metastasis."
L53: 
L54: ​
L55: 
L56: Oct 28, 2024: Veterinary Cancer Society Meeting
L57: 
L58:   * Almost 12-month median survival time was reported for osteosarcoma patients who received palliative radiation plus vaccine WITHOUT amputation.
L59: 
L60:   * Longer median survival times (compared to chemotherapy alone) were reported for Stage 1 and Stage 2 hemangiosarcoma canine patients.
L61: 
L62: ​​
L63: They are early results with a small number of patients. More data is being collected.​​​
L64: 
L65: ​
L66: 
L67: An Introductory 【5†Quick Guide on Canine Cancer Immunotherapy can be downloaded here†ccralliance.myflodesk.com】.​
L68: 
L69: 【9†Image: Maggie 2023.jpg†static.wixstatic.com】
L70: 
L71: Maggie was diagnosed with osteosarcoma in Jan 2020 and got conventional treatment plus the vaccine.  She is still cancer-free.
L72: 
L73: 【10†Image: ranger_edited.jpg†static.wixstatic.com】
L74: Ranger's cancer kept on spreading, even after surgery and chemotherapy.  But his tumors shrank and disappeared after the EGFR/HER2 vaccine treatment.
L75: 
L76: 【11†Image: Codi_edited.jpg†static.wixstatic.com】
L77: 
L78: Codi's metastatic osteosarcoma began to disappear a month after he received the EGFR/HER2 vaccine injection. He enjoyed 3 extra years as a healthy, happy pup.
L79: 
L80: 【12†Learn More】
L81: # How does it work?
L82: 
L83:   * Safely activates the immune system against cancer cells that are over-expressing EGFR and HER2 proteins.
L84: 
L85:   * 【12†The vaccine has already been given to over 600 canine patients】. Minimum side effects reported.
L86: 
L87:   * May help with many different cancer types. Preliminary data for osteosarcoma and hemangiosarcoma published.
L88: 
L89:   * Watch a recent update from the team.
L90: # Limitations and Challenges
L91: 
L92:   * Today's immunotherapy cannot guarantee every dog will become a long-term survivor.
L93: 
L94:   * Researchers are investigating different ways to safely enhance the efficacy and increase the number of responders.
L95: 
L96: # Learn about strategies that might enhance efficacy of immunotherapy treatments.

L5: # Projects
L6: 
L7: 【2†Image: Jewell hemangiosarcoma.jpg†static.wixstatic.com】
L8: 
L9: Canine Cancer Alliance accelerates the discovery of safer and much more effective treatments for dogs with cancer.
L10: 
L11: ​
L12: 
L13: By funding research, supporting clinical trials, and empowering families with the latest findings, CCA is helping end dog cancer as we know it today.
L14: 
L15: 【3†Image†static.wixstatic.com】
L16: 
L17: Prof.  Mamula  with Ranger who became cancer-free after his metastatic osteosarcoma was treated with the vaccine.
L18: 
L19: ​
L20: # EGFR/HE R2 C anine Cancer Vaccine
L21: 
L22: ​
L23: 
L24: A clinical trial is open at ten locations  for canine patients with osteosarcoma, hemangiosarcoma and TCC which are cancer types often associated with EGFR/HER2 overexpression.  See 【4†the status page】 to find out which clinics are participating in the study.  Please contact the clinic directly to find out the requirement and to request an appointment.
L25: 
L26: ​
L27: 
L28: Learn more about the potential 【5†benefits of the vaccine including prevention of metastasis here.】
L29: 
L30: ​
L31: 
L32: ​
L33: # Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Combination Therapy
L34: 
L35: ​
L36: 
L37: Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor (ICI) treatments work by blocking the inhibitory signals that cancer cells use to evade detection by immune cells.
L38: 
L39: 
L40: 
L41: ICI has shown remarkable success in treating various types of cancer in human medicine.
L42: 
L43: 
L44: 
L45: CCA is supporting a number of projects that combine the use of ICI with other immune modulating therapies.
L46: 
L47: ​
L48: 
L49: 【6†Image: Golden Dog†static.wixstatic.com】
L50: 
L51: ​
L52: # Gut Microbiome and Cancer
L53: 
L54: ​
L55: 
L56: With human patients, researchers can now correlate 【7†successful immunotherapy response to the patient's gut microbiome composition】.
L57: This study will analyze the gut microbiome from canine patients receiving immunotherapy treatments at multiple  time points during their treatment.  The ultimate goal is to to be able to help more cancer patients respond to immunotherapy and survive longer through modulation of the microbiome, for example, via diet change or with the help of fecal transplant.
L58: 
L59: 
L60: 
L61: This study is a collaborative effort between Oregon State University, Yale University and private clinics.
L62: 
L63: ​
L64: 
L65: 【8†Image†static.wixstatic.com】
L66: ​
L67: # Fasting and Immune Modulation
L68: 
L69: ​
L70: 
L71: Short term fasting can dramatically relieve the side effects in cancer patients - people ad dogs - undergoing chemotherapy. Cyclic fasting has also been shown to help activate the anti-tumorigenic immune response in human cancer patients. (See this 【9†summary】).  This is the first of a series of studies investigating impact of dietary intervention added to conventional or experimental therapy.
L72: This study is a collaborative effort between Ohio State University and Oregon State University.
L73: 
L74: ​
L75: 
L76: 【10†Image: Dog†static.wixstatic.com】
L77: 
L78: ​
L79: # CAR-T Therapy for Solid Tumors
L80: 
L81: ​
L82: 
L83: With CAR-T immunotherapy, the patient's T-cells are modified so that they can target cancer cells much more effectively.   The potential of CAR-T therapy has been demonstrated in treating human blood cancers, but not in solid tumors or in canine patients.
L84: This study is exploring how CAR-T therapy targeting B7H3 receptors might be used to treat solid tumors to help canine patients.   A collaborative effort between Northwestern University and University of Illinois teams, 【11†the trial is now enrolling patients with hemangiosarcoma.†vetmed.illinois.edu】
L85: 
L86: ​
L87: ###### Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR)-T therapy works by modifying the immune cells called T cells (a type of white blood cell) to find and fight cancer much more effectively.
L88: 
L89: ​
L90: # Nonspecific Immune Stimulating Therapy
L91: 
L92: ​
L93: 
L94: The ongoing pilot trial is evaluating the efficacy of mycobacterial cell wall fraction (MCWF) - 【12†Immunocidin - in slowing or preventing metastasis of dogs】 with osteosarcoma and other aggressive solid tumors.
L95: 
L96: ​
L97: 
L98: An additional new study for Transitional Cell Carcinoma (Bladder Cancer) canine patients, in collaboration with North Carolina State University, is enrolling canine patients.
L99: 
L100: 【13†Image: Rigsby fibrosarcoma canine patient.png†static.wixstatic.com】
L101: After 1-year old Rigsby was diagnosed with fibrosarcoma, his vet began treating him with Immunocidin as part of a new study.
L102: 
L103: 【14†Image: cytokines and immunotherapy.png†static.wixstatic.com】

L48: ### Exploratory Field Trial to Investigate Efficacy and Safety of BI 705564 in Dogs with B-cell Lymphoma
L49: 
L50: CURRENTLY ENROLLING
L51: #### SUMMARY OF STUDY:
L52: 
L53: Lymphoma is the most common malignancy in dogs, with B-cell lymphomas accounting for ~70% of all canine lymphomas. There is an unmet need for effective treatments for canine B-cell lymphoma. The standard of care for dogs with B-cell lymphoma provides relatively short median overall survival times despite high remission rates. Side effects are common and may be dose-limiting.
L54: B-cell lymphoma occurs as a result of neoplastic transformation and clonal expansion of B-lymphocytes. Aberrant expression of multiple components of B-cell receptor (BCR) signaling has been demonstrated in canine B-cell lymphoma. Bruton’s tyrosine kinase (BTK) plays a crucial role in oncogenic signaling downstream of the BCR that is critical for the proliferation and survival of B-cells in many B-cell malignancies.
L55: The BTK inhibitor BI 705564 has the potential to achieve marked clinical responses in dogs with B-cell malignancies and addresses major unmet needs. These include the expected improvement of quality of life with minimal side effects, increased survival time, oral administration, and affordability. These characteristics will empower general practitioners to treat canine lymphoma and increase accessibility to care for dogs with lymphoma.
L56: This study will evaluate the efficacy and safety of BI 705564 in dogs with treatment-naïve B-cell lymphoma.
L57: #### INCLUSION CRITERIA:
L58: 
L59: Dogs >1 year of age and weighing between 10-50 kg
L60: 
L61: At least two lymph nodes measuring >2 cm in largest diameter
L62: 
L63: Dogs cannot have received systemic corticosteroid treatment for more than 2 weeks and/or within 5 days prior to screening
L64: 
L65: No prior chemotherapy (cytotoxic chemotherapy, verdinexor/Laverdia) or radiation therapy.
L66: 
L67: No current immunotherapy treatment (e.g. monoclonal antibodies: beimvetmab/Librela, lokivetmab/Cytopoint).
L68: 
L69: Stage II, III, or IV B-cell lymphoma
L70: #### FINANCIAL INCENTIVES:
L71: 
L72: Participating pet owners will receive:
L73: 
L74: Screening testing, including blood work, urinalysis, chest x-rays, abdominal ultrasound, flow cytometry, and IDEXX Cancer Dx Panel are covered. Once enrolled, the study is fully funded.
L75: #### WHAT TO EXPECT:
L76: 
L77: Participating patients will be required to complete standard pre-enrollment screening that involves a physical exam, blood work, urinalysis, lymph node testing, radiographs, and ultrasound. Dogs are seen weekly, then every 2 weeks for a study duration of 12 weeks. Owners will administer oral BI 705565 daily with a meal. We will monitor blood work and lymph node size to evaluate safety and efficacy.
L78:

L4: CASTR: Companion Animal Studies for Translational Research
L5: 
L6: 【2†Ongoing Studies】 【3†Contact】
L7: ## What we do
L8: 
L9: CASTR Alliance aims to advance human and veterinary medicine by facilitating the discovery of innovative treatments through the management of high-quality veterinary clinical studies and collaboration with industry leaders and veterinary hospitals.
L10: 
L11: We provide turnkey management of sponsored veterinary clinical studies to pharmaceutical and medical device development teams worldwide.
L12: We partner with state-of-the-art veterinary specialty and referral hospitals throughout the Pacific Northwest and beyond to enroll patients on sponsored clinical studies.
L13: 
L14: We manage sponsored clinical trials that abide by Good Clinical Practice (GCP) standards for veterinary studies and are designed to ensure the collection of high-quality data.
L15: We submit all CASTR-run studies for ethical review by an external Veterinary Clinical Studies Committee (VCSC) to prioritize the safety and well-being of all patients.
L16: 
L17: 【4†MORE DETAILS】
L18: ## What motivates us
L19: 
L20: The motivations behind CASTR Alliance’s efforts are to connect companion animals with cutting-edge treatments, address naturally occurring diseases in pets, and accelerate medical innovation for both animals and humans through clinical trials.
L21: 
L22: #### Linking Patients to Caregivers
L23: 
L24: Our sponsored studies link companion animals in need of innovative solutions to novel therapeutic or diagnostic options that may otherwise be unavailable to them.
L25: #### Studying Spontaneous Diseases
L26: 
L27: Our research focuses on spontaneous diseases – those that arise naturally in dogs and cats. By enrolling companion animals who are already afflicted or symptomatic, we aim to provide potential direct benefits to our pets while gathering data that could help human or animal patients in the future.
L28: 
L29: #### Accelerating Medical Innovation
L30: 
L31: When a pet is enrolled in a CASTR-managed clinical trial, they take part in helping advance medical discovery and innovation.
L32: ## 【5†Translational research:】 Caring for our pets while advancing human and animal healthcare
L33: 
L34: ## What to expect
L35: 
L36: #### Contracting companies
L37: 
L38: can expect all CASTR Alliance-run studies to be managed efficiently and ethically, adhere to GCP standards, and result in high quality data. We deliver progress updates upon request throughout the trial, conduct diligent site and safety monitoring, and provide data at interim analysis, and at the conclusion of the trial.
L39: #### Veterinary clinicians
L40: 
L41: and support staff participating in the study are trained from the onset on the trial protocol to ensure treatment is conducted according to our rigorous standards. We continue to provide guidance and support to our participating sites throughout the entire course of the study.
L42: #### Pet owners
L43: 
L44: who enroll their pets in these clinical studies engage directly with a participating veterinary center, where all study procedures are carried out in accordance with the established study protocol. Studies are typically supported such that treatment is partially or fully covered by the sponsor.
L45: ## WHO WE ARE
L46: CASTR Alliance was founded in 2019 by veterinary clinician-scientists Jessica Bertout and Jim Perry. As scientists, they bring extensive experience in designing, managing, and conducting clinical trials that meet the rigorous standards of the biotech industry. Moreover, as devoted pet owners and veterinarians, they are personally committed to delivering the highest quality care for our animal companions. Together, Drs.
L47: Bertout and Perry created CASTR Alliance to leverage their expertise and advance medicine for humans and animals alike.

L36: # Current Clinical Trials
L37: Our clinical trials program is one of the largest in veterinary oncology and is supported by seven dedicated staff members. Annually, the program manages an average of 30 clinical trials to study more effective therapies for a variety of cancer types including, osteosarcoma, lymphoma, soft tissue sarcoma, and brain tumors. The following trials are currently enrolling patients. For more information, please contact the clinical trials service at (970) 297-4001 or email 【28†[email protected]】.
L38: In general, to participate in one of our clinical trials, patients must be treated at our facility, but will go home after each appointment, unless the protocol dictates otherwise. Most families who participate in our clinical trials live within 150 miles of Fort Collins or are willing to travel or temporarily relocate for the period of the study.
L39: Clinical trials related to pet cancer are conducted throughout the United States. If you do not live close enough to participate in one of our trials, please visit the 【29†AVMA Veterinary Clinical Trials Registry website†veterinaryclinicaltrials.org】 to search for trials in your area.

L111: ## One Cure for pets and people with cancer
L112: 
L113: 【40†Image: Connie And Leo With Logo】
L114: 
L115: Funding for our clinical trials program comes from generous donors to our 【14†One Cure】 initiative. One Cure’s founding principle is that cancer affects all creatures, and that treatment breakthroughs come through collaboration between scientists and doctors who are working with both pets and people. One Cure’s goal is to raise awareness and monetary support for clinical trials and comparative oncology research.
